subject: Finishes that connect living spaces
hook: A finish plan takes five decisions. Most people make them in the wrong order.
ig:
A finish plan takes five decisions. Most people make them in the wrong order.

The usual mistake is falling for a door colour first, then trying to make the floor and worktop fit around it. Here's the order we'd work in for a typical open-plan home:

1. List what's staying: floor, worktop, fireplace, internal doors.
2. Choose a lead finish that works with all of them.
3. Add a single accent for living-room pieces.
4. Decide on handles once and use them everywhere.
5. Test samples in your own light before committing.

Then everything is made to that plan in our own workshop, so the sideboard, shelving and media wall all match what you signed off.

Doing it in this order stops the expensive bit, the furniture, from clashing with the things you're not replacing.

Save this one, and see finished rooms via the link in bio.
fb:
Planning furniture for an open-plan room? Try doing it in this order: first list what you're keeping (floor, worktop, fireplace), then pick a lead finish that suits them, add one accent, settle on a handle, and test it all in your own daylight.

It sounds obvious, but most clashes happen when the door colour gets picked first. Once the plan is set, every piece is made to it in our workshop.

on_asset:
F1: List what stays — Flooring, worktops, fireplace, doors. These are fixed, so every new finish has to work with them. |
F2: Choose the lead finish — The largest surface in the space, often kitchen doors, sets the base colour and sheen. |
F3: Add one accent — A contrasting finish for shelving, a media wall or a sideboard. Warm against cool works well. |
F4: Fix the hardware — Antique gold or matt black, used the same way across every room. |
F5: Test in your light — Samples on your floor, by the window and in the shade, at different times of day. |
F6: Made to the plan — Every piece is cut, edged and assembled in our workshop to the agreed finish schedule. |
